title: Lesson Pace: Reducing Friction in Classrooms
author: Ben Cooper
summary: Primary teacher and writer Ben Cooper reframes the vague observation feedback that 'the lesson needed more pace'. He argues that pace is not speed but sharpness, achieved by removing the small, frequent frictions that eat classroom time, such as broken pens, unclear routines, muddled instructions and unseen time limits. He offers four levers: build familiarity through taught routines like Show Me and Turn and Talk, remove physical friction by giving resources clear homes and prepping them in advance, sharpen communication with short instructions and consistent cues, and use visual timers to make time concrete. Cooper then adds a counterweight, drawing on Bjork's desirable difficulties: teachers should not remove useful friction, and should slow down when checks for understanding show pupils are not yet secure.
points: Pace means a lesson with very little in the way, not a rushed one, so the goal is to reduce unnecessary friction rather than to talk or work faster.
Taught and rehearsed routines such as Show Me, cold calling and Turn and Talk free working memory because pupils no longer have to work out how to participate.
Clear homes for resources, pre-placed whiteboards and grouped trays remove many minute-long interruptions, and visiting other classrooms is a cheap way to learn these systems.
Economical instructions, familiar gestures and visual timers make expectations clear and create positive urgency rather than anxiety.
Desirable difficulties should be protected, so a failed check for understanding is a cue to slow down and re-teach, not to keep moving.
quotes: When I personally think about pace, I tend to think about lessons not being rushed, but instead being sharp. After all, we don’t want rushed lessons or learning.
A well-paced classroom, therefore, is not necessarily one where tasks are moving quickly from one to the next like a train that rumbles on. It is, instead, one where very little gets in the way.
The aim isn’t achieving zero friction. It is trying to reduce friction as much as possible.
Familiarity is a key to pace. If children are unfamiliar with the routines and expectations, or how to participate within a lesson, we are allowing for unnecessary friction.

Frequently used resources need clear and explicit homes. Pupils need to know how to access these resources, replace them if they are no longer working, and how to put them away so that they’re ready to access again the next time they are needed.
Time is an abstract concept. Without a visible reference point, pupils can struggle to judge how quickly they need to work or how much time remains.

Missing a whiteboard pen is not desirable. Giving children an extra minute to retrieve previously learned knowledge and really unpick and wrestle with some key concepts and ideas, or to reconsider an incorrect answer, is a desirable difficulty we want to encourage.
